title: Two news openings: the same protest
stem:
Two openings of news reports about the same event, from two different (fictional) outlets.

TEXT A — The Daily Standard
CHAOS AS MOB BRINGS CITY TO STANDSTILL
Thousands of commuters were left stranded yesterday after a mob of activists blocked Westbridge for six hours. Furious workers missed shifts and hospital appointments as police struggled to contain the unruly crowd. 'It's a disgrace,' said one taxi driver.

TEXT B — The Westbridge Voice
YOUNG RESIDENTS MARCH FOR CLEAN AIR
Around 3,000 people, many of them students, marched peacefully across Westbridge yesterday to demand action on the city's air pollution, which a council report links to 140 early deaths a year. 'We're marching for our lungs,' said Priya, 17, holding a hand-painted placard.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Compare how the two headlines and opening sentences represent the protesters.
markscheme: Text A: 'mob' and 'unruly crowd' connote disorder and threat; Text B: 'residents', 'students', 'marched peacefully' connote legitimacy
Text A 'CHAOS' and 'STANDSTILL': capitalised, emotive framing on disruption; Text B frames the purpose ('for clean air')
Text A focuses on victims (commuters, workers, patients) – the protesters' cause is omitted
Text B omits disruption to commuters entirely – both texts select and omit
numbers: A's vague 'thousands' vs B's 'around 3,000' and attributed statistic – different ethos
voices quoted: anonymous angry taxi driver vs named, young protester – shapes sympathy

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Discuss what each text's choices suggest about its implied reader and values.
markscheme: Text A implies a reader who values order, work and convenience, possibly sceptical of activism
Text B implies a local reader concerned with health and sympathetic to young people's activism
both outlets' framing reflects ideology/bias rather than neutral reporting
recognises that readers can resist the implied position
